title: SigmaDock: Molecular Docking with Fragment-Based Diffusion
one_liner: Breaking a drug molecule into rigid pieces and reassembling them in a protein pocket using a step-by-step diffusion process beats hand-written rules.
lead: When a drug molecule (ligand) binds to a protein, it must fit into the protein's binding pocket in exactly the right shape and position. Predicting this binding pose is called molecular docking, and it is critical for drug discovery. Classical methods rely on hand-coded physics rules and are slow but reliable. Recent neural networks promise speed and diversity but produce impossible geometries and fail on new proteins. SigmaDock breaks the ligand into rigid-body fragments (like puzzle pieces), then uses a generative process to learn how to reassemble them in the correct pose.

problem.h2: Why deep learning for docking fails
paras: A naive deep learning approach takes a protein and a ligand as inputs and tries to predict the final 3D pose (position and rotation) directly. The problem: molecules have rigid structure. The atoms within the ligand cannot move freely; they are held together by chemical bonds at fixed distances and angles. A neural network trained end-to-end does not know this, so it generates poses where bonds stretch, angles distort, and atoms collide. The result is chemically impossible.

Worse, these networks are trained on thousands of protein-ligand complexes in the lab, but real drug discovery needs to dock ligands into completely new proteins. The network overfits to protein families it has seen before and fails on unfamiliar targets. Building a single end-to-end model that handles both geometric plausibility and generalization is hard because the network must learn chemistry implicitly, without being told what chemistry is.

callout.b: The core problem in one sentence.
callout.html: Neural networks generate chemically impossible geometries and fail to generalize because they do not respect molecular structure.

steps.text: Break the input drug molecule into rigid-body pieces, preserving bond lengths and angles.
Place fragments randomly rotated and positioned inside the protein pocket.
Neural network sees noisy fragment positions and predicts where they should be.
Subtract the predicted noise, moving fragments closer to their real positions each step.
After many steps, fragments align to form the correct binding pose with chemistry intact.

paras: Instead of predicting the full 3D pose all at once, SigmaDock learns to refine fragment positions and rotations one small step at a time. Each step moves the fragments closer to plausible configurations that respect the chemical constraints of the molecule and fit inside the protein pocket.

hidden.name: Geometric constraint satisfaction
paras: Every atom in a molecule is held at a precise distance and angle from its neighbors by chemical bonds. The paper names this implicitly: the fragments must stay rigid, and must satisfy soft geometric constraints (the bond lengths and angles do not stretch beyond their natural ranges). This is the hidden quantity—the degree to which a proposed fragment arrangement respects the molecule's structure.

SigmaDock measures this using soft potential-energy penalties. When a fragment's rotation strays from a valid orientation, or when fragments are positioned too close to break chemical bonds, a penalty accumulates. During training (adjusting the network), the network learns to predict the score (which direction to move fragments to reduce penalties). During inference (when the finished model answers a new question), the refinement steps follow these direction predictions toward chemically valid configurations.

heat.caption: Darker means more constraint satisfaction; highlights mark the core chemical-validity signal.

reads.html: The model learns to nudge fragments toward arrangements where bonds do not stretch and atoms do not collide.
SE(3) Riemannian diffusion parametrizes the score of the data distribution; soft holonomic constraints (force-constant penalties) provide implicit boundary conditions.

paras: Classical physics-based docking uses hand-written force fields (energy models) to score poses. These are accurate but slow. End-to-end neural networks are fast but ignore chemistry, producing impossible outputs. SigmaDock splits the difference by baking chemistry into the problem structure, not the network weights. By decomposing the ligand into rigid fragments, the network never has to learn 'how to make valid molecules'—that constraint is built in. Fragments cannot bend, so bad configurations are already ruled out. Soft constraints (weak penalties) on bond angles and distances guide the network toward plausible configurations without hard constraints that break learning.

The diffusion process (iterative refinement) is the key. In a single-step network, the model must predict all fragment positions at once, a hard combinatorial problem. In diffusion, the network predicts only the direction to nudge fragments given their current noisy positions. This is easier: the network learns a local correction, not a global guess. Over many steps, local nudges accumulate into a coherent final pose. Generalization works because the network learns the shape of the constraint space (where penalties are low and poses are valid), not memorized protein shapes. A new protein has a different binding pocket structure, but the same forces push fragments to fit and the same bonds to preserve.

stages.s: Encode protein structure and fragment state
Predict score: direction to move each fragment
Refine: subtract noise, apply soft chemical penalties
Final fragment poses forming chemically valid binding configuration

math.words: penalty = sum over bonds of (force-constant times angle-deviation-squared plus distance-deviation-squared)
math.equation: L(z_t) = sum_bonds k_AB * (angle_error)^2 + k_ABC * (distance_error)^2 + lambda_t * ||score_predicted - score_true||^2
symbols: fragment positions and rotations at noise level t
penalty strength for bonds and angles
the true direction to move (gradient of the data distribution)
what the network learns to predict
loss scaling (stronger penalty at high noise)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose Fragment A has a bond to Fragment B at ideal angle 120 degrees.
Noisy fragment positions give angle 110 degrees (deviation 10 degrees).
Penalty on this bond: 50 * 10^2 = 5000 (large, because deviation is large).
Network predicts: rotate fragment A by +3 degrees.
After update, angle becomes 113 degrees (deviation 7 degrees).
Over 50 steps, penalties shrink monotonically toward valid configurations.

math.note: The force-constant penalty prevents bad configurations; diffusion steps gradually align fragment positions to satisfy these constraints.

items.html: If the initial fragmentation breaks the molecule into pieces that are too flexible (not rigid), the constraint signal is weak and the network must learn to suppress illegal motions, defeating the point of fragmentation.

If the protein binding pocket is much larger than the training distribution (e.g. a ligand docking into an oversized cavity), the model has not learned the constraint space in that regime and may place fragments incorrectly even if chemistry is satisfied.
Diffusion processes are sensitive to loss weighting across noise levels. Poor scaling makes the network ignore high-noise steps or over-focus on tiny refinements, breaking convergence.

With careful fragmentation (preserving rigidity), soft constraints (not hard walls), and adaptive loss scaling, SigmaDock generalizes: new proteins are handled correctly as long as the binding pocket is within the learned distribution.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: A minimal demo takes a protein structure (PDB file) and a drug molecule (SMILES string), splits the ligand into fragments using the paper's fragmentation algorithm, samples 10 random initial poses from a noise distribution, runs 50 diffusion steps (network predicts fragment corrections at each step), and measures the final pose quality using two metrics: (a) RMSD (how far the predicted pose sits from the crystal structure), and (b) chemical plausibility (are bond angles within 10 degrees of valid, are atoms farther than van-der-Waals radius). The demo should show that all 10 samples converge to valid geometries near the ground truth, even though they started from random noise.
demo.metric_eq: Top-1 accuracy = fraction of trials where best-of-10 poses achieve RMSD < 2A and all bonds within 10 degrees of valid geometry
demo.closing: The demo makes impossible to miss: fragments lock into place respecting chemistry, and even random starts converge to the same plausible pose, proving the method is learning the constraint space, not memorizing protein shapes.
